topic: Classifying geometric and p-series; the nth-term test

problems.desc: The second half of problem 1: a correct response reads the table as evidence that the partial sums are climbing toward a ceiling near 1.5 and getting there quickly, and then says that the table can only suggest a limit while the geometric-series formula proves it. Full credit makes that distinction between numerical evidence and proof.

Part (b): a correct response states the nth-term test in the only direction it works --- if the terms do not approach zero the series diverges --- and applies it here, where the terms approach three fifths. Full credit also says what the test would NOT have told us if the limit had been zero.

problems.slot: the distance after the first drop

problems.desc: Part (b): a correct response says a p-series converges exactly when the exponent p exceeds one, and that here p equals four. Full credit connects that to the table --- the partial sums settle quickly because the terms shrink faster than one over n --- rather than only quoting the rule.

Part (b): a correct response notes that the individual terms approach one rather than zero, so the nth-term test applies and the series diverges. Full credit explains why the terms do not shrink --- the factor n grows exactly as fast as the sine shrinks --- instead of only reporting the limit.

Part (b): a correct response says every repeating decimal can be written the same way --- the repeating block over a power of ten, times a geometric series with ratio one over that power of ten --- and a geometric series with a rational first term and rational ratio always sums to a rational number. Full credit gives that general argument, not just a second worked example.

problems.slot: the sum of the first series
the limit for the third series

problems.desc: Part (c): a correct response classifies all three --- the first converges as a geometric series with ratio two thirds, the second diverges as a p-series with exponent one half, and the third diverges by the nth-term test since its terms approach one. Full credit names the deciding quantity for each (the ratio, the exponent, the limit of the terms) rather than only the verdict.
